title: Pipeline evaluation mechanisms and metrics · Reliable and safe trustworthy software architectures

slides.title: Recap: Automated Testing Mechanisms
slides.notes: Briefly remind students of the testing taxonomy covered in Week 10. Emphasise that AI‑native pipelines add non‑deterministic components, so traditional pass/fail gates are insufficient. Mention the shift from static test suites to continuous metric collection.

slides.title: Why Evaluate AI‑Native Pipelines?
slides.notes: Explain that evaluation is not a one‑off activity; it must run continuously because models evolve. Highlight that reliability requirements (availability, latency bounds, safety) translate directly into measurable pipeline metrics.

slides.title: Core Evaluation Metric Categories
slides.notes: Walk through each category, linking to concrete tools (e.g., HuggingFace evaluate, Prometheus for latency). Stress that a single metric never tells the whole story; a portfolio is required for trustworthy deployment.

slides.title: Metric Trade‑offs in Practice
bullets: Fairness checks may conflict with accuracy
slides.notes: Use the flow to illustrate how teams negotiate competing objectives. Cite the cross‑model study (C1) showing that complexity backpressure forces explicit trade‑off decisions in AI coding agents.

slides.title: Aligning Metrics to Reliability Requirements
bullets: Map each SLA to a measurable metric
slides.notes: Show a template: Requirement → Metric → Threshold → Monitoring. Emphasise traceability: every design decision in the pipeline must reference at least one reliability requirement, a core expectation for LO2.

slides.title: Check: Metric Selection

quiz.question: A pipeline must guarantee 99.9 % availability and sub‑200 ms p99 latency. Which metric set best satisfies both?
quiz.explanation: Option 1 (index 1) directly measures the two stated SLAs: latency percentile and error rate (availability). The other sets miss at least one SLA.

slides.notes: Poll the class, then discuss why latency and error‑rate are the primary indicators for the given SLAs. Clarify that cost and fairness are secondary concerns here.

slides.title: Activity: Define Metrics for Sample Pipeline
slides.notes: Students work in pairs on a fictitious AI‑native service (e.g., code‑generation API). They produce a one‑page metric‑requirement map. Instructor circulates to probe justification.

slides.title: Principles of Trustworthy AI‑Native Architectures
slides.notes: Introduce the four pillars from recent trustworthy‑AI literature. Connect each pillar to concrete architectural mechanisms (logging, sandboxing, policy engines). This frames the design decisions students must justify in LO2.

slides.title: Safety Layers: Guardrails, Monitoring, Fallback
slides.notes: Walk through the flow: every request passes guardrails, then monitoring; anomalies trigger fallback. Stress that each layer addresses a distinct reliability requirement (integrity, availability, safety).

slides.title: Reliability Patterns: Circuit Breaker, Retry, Idempotency
bullets: Exponential back‑off retry for transient errors
slides.notes: Explain each pattern with a one‑sentence scenario. Show how they map to requirements: circuit breaker → availability, retry → latency bound, idempotency → data consistency. Mention that AI‑native steps (model inference) often need custom timeouts.

slides.title: Designing a Testing Pipeline for Multi‑Component Projects
slides.notes: Detail the rationale for each stage. Emphasise that contract tests catch schema drift early, while end‑to‑end simulation validates the full reliability envelope. This pipeline is the artefact students will assess in the worked problem.

slides.title: Worked Problem: Assess Pipeline Against Reliability Requirements
bullets: Map each pipeline stage to metrics

figure.caption: Sample pipeline config (excerpt)
figure.code:
stages:
  - name: unit_test
    script: pytest unit/
  - name: integration_test
    script: pytest integration/
  - name: contract_test
    script: pact-verifier
  - name: e2e_sim
    script: run_sim.sh
  - name: metrics_collect
    script: collect_metrics.py

slides.notes: Step through the assessment: (1) list requirements, (2) trace each to a metric collected in metrics_collect, (3) notice the inference stage lacks a circuit breaker, (4) propose a fallback model stage with its own latency budget, (5) define alert rules (e.g., error‑rate >0.1 % triggers paging). This demonstrates the justification skill required for LO2.

slides.title: Check: Missing Reliability Requirement

quiz.question: In the worked problem, which reliability requirement was not addressed by the original pipeline?
quiz.explanation: The original config had no circuit‑breaker stage for model inference, leaving the system vulnerable to cascade failures. Latency and availability were covered by metrics; cost was out of scope.

slides.notes: Quick poll, then reinforce that architectural patterns (circuit breaker) are explicit design decisions that must be traced to a requirement.

slides.title: Activity: Group Design of Pipeline Architecture
bullets: Sketch a pipeline with safety layers
Annotate each stage with a requirement
slides.notes: Groups produce a one‑page diagram (paper or digital). Instructor evaluates whether every stage cites a requirement and whether patterns like circuit breaker, fallback, and audit log appear. This mirrors the project milestone assessment.

slides.title: Summary: Key Takeaways
bullets: Evaluation metrics must map 1‑to‑1 to reliability SLAs
Trade‑offs are explicit decisions, not accidents
Trustworthy architectures layer guardrails, monitoring, fallbacks
Reliability patterns (circuit breaker, retry, idempotency) are mandatory
Every pipeline design choice needs a documented justification
slides.notes: Recap the two lecture parts. Remind students that the project milestone (due Week 12) requires a full pipeline assessment with justifications. Point to the lab next week for hands‑on metric implementation.
